bullets: Workhouses were made deliberately **harsh** to discourage people from relying on them (‘less eligibility’).
Families were **separated** (men, women, children in different wards).
Food was minimal, work hard and repetitive (breaking stones, picking oakum), and uniforms stigmatising.
Many poor people would rather starve than enter: hence the charity collectors’ reply that ‘many would rather die’.
Debtors could be imprisoned; the **treadmill** was a prison punishment.

callouts.p: ‘Are there no prisons?’ … ‘And the Union workhouses? … Are they still in operation?’ Scrooge believes paying taxes for these institutions ends his responsibility. Dickens makes the reader hear how cold this is.

core.p: Before 1834, parishes gave ‘outdoor relief’ (money or food) to the poor. The **New Poor Law** ended most of this: able-bodied poor people who needed help had to enter a **workhouse**.

bullets: Scrooge: ‘If they would rather die, they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.’
In Stave 3 the Ghost of Christmas Present throws these words back when Scrooge asks if Tiny Tim will live: ‘If he be like to die, he had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.’
The Ghost then rebukes him: ‘forbear that wicked cant until you have discovered What the surplus is, and Where it is.’
Dickens turns an abstract theory into a named, loved child, so the reader feels the cruelty of the idea.
core.p: Thomas **Malthus**, in An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), argued that population grows faster than food supply, so poverty and death were natural checks.

bullets: **Stave 1**: Scrooge voices Poor Law and Malthusian views: the reader is positioned to judge him.
**Stave 3**: the views are repeated against Tiny Tim and Ignorance and Want (‘Are there no prisons? Are there no workhouses?’): **cyclical structure** punishes Scrooge with his own words.
**Stave 5**: Scrooge whispers a large donation to the charity collector: he takes personal responsibility rather than relying on institutions.

model: Scrooge’s Stave 1 views (prisons, workhouses, surplus population)
exam.q: Explain how Dickens presents attitudes to poverty elsewhere in the novella. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Show how attitudes change, not just what they are.

mistakes.r: They were deliberately harsh and feared.
The Ghost repeats Scrooge’s words: a key structural point.

quotes.a: Cold reliance on institutions; rhetorical question.
The Ghost rebukes Scrooge with his own words.
quotes.q: What the surplus is, and Where it is

summary: The 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act forced the poor into harsh workhouses, and Malthus’s idea of ‘surplus population’ justified neglect; Dickens attacks both through Scrooge’s words in Stave 1 and their reversal in Stave 3.

terms.d: An institution where the poor received food and shelter in exchange for hard labour.
Help given to the poor in their own homes, mostly abolished in 1834.
Based on Malthus’s ideas that population must be checked by hunger and disease.
